llm.text: The exact causes for developing asthma are unknown and may differ between individuals [P1]. Asthma can occur when the body’s natural defenses react strongly to a new substance in the lungs [P1]. Factors such as early‑life exposure to environmental allergens, cigarette smoke, certain germs, viral infections, and family history can raise the risk of developing asthma [P1]. Being overweight can increase the risk of developing asthma or make symptoms worse [P3]. Certain racial or ethnic groups, such as Puerto Rican and Black or African American people, have a higher risk of developing asthma [P3]. Occupational exposure to chemicals or industrial dust can also raise the risk of developing asthma [P3].

llm.text:
Chest tightness is a common sign of asthma [P1].  
Coughing, especially at night or early in the morning, is a typical sign [P1].  
Shortness of breath or breathlessness can indicate asthma [P1][P4].  
Wheezing, a whistling sound when breathing out, is a usual sign of asthma [P1][P2].  
These symptoms may occur every day or only occasionally [P1].  
Symptoms often get worse at night or in the morning and may be triggered by infections, exercise, allergies, cold air, or strong emotions [P2].

extractive.text: It can be hard to tell if someone has asthma, especially in children under age 5. [P1] A doctor can help you find out if you have asthma. [P1] He or she may ask whether anyone in your family has or has had asthma, allergies, or other breathing problems. [P1]

llm.text:
Doctors ask about coughing, especially at night, breathing problems after activity or at certain times of year, chest tightness, wheezing, long‑lasting colds, family history of asthma or allergies, and how symptoms affect school, work, or daily activities [P1].  
They also perform a breathing test called spirometry, which measures how much air you can exhale before and after using asthma medicine [P1].  
Healthcare providers may use a physical exam, review your medical history, and conduct lung‑function tests such as spirometry and peak expiratory flow testing to see how well your lungs work [P2].  
They can test how your airways react to specific exposures by having you inhale different concentrations of allergens or medicines and then repeat spirometry [P2].  
Allergy skin or blood tests may be done to identify triggers, and fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) tests may measure airway inflammation [P2].  
Additional tests such as blood tests for white‑blood‑cell levels or a chest CT scan can also help assess inflammation and airway changes [P4].

You should seek care right away if you have been hospitalized for asthma in the past year or had a life‑threatening asthma attack in the past [P1].  
You should also call right away if you recently needed oral corticosteroids to treat asthma or are not using inhaled corticosteroids [P1].  
Using more than one canister of a short‑acting beta2‑agonist reliever each month is another reason to contact your provider immediately [P1].  
If you have a mental health condition, an alcohol or drug use disorder, do not closely follow your asthma action plan, or have a food allergy, you should call your provider right away [P1].  
For young children with asthma, call 9‑1‑1 if they seem drowsy, confused, troubled, have a blue tint to skin or lips, or have a fast heartbeat [P1].  
If your asthma medicines do not relieve an asthma attack or your peak flow number is low, you should also contact your provider right away [P1].

llm.text: The A1C test is a blood test that provides information about your average blood‑glucose levels over the past three months [P2]. It measures how much glucose is attached to hemoglobin in red blood cells, reflecting the average glucose level during that time [P2]. Large changes in blood glucose over the past month affect the A1C result more than changes in earlier months [P1]. The test is used to diagnose type 2 diabetes, prediabetes, and to manage diabetes [P2]. For most people with diabetes, the goal is an A1C level below 7% [P3]. The A1C result does not show sudden, temporary increases or decreases in blood glucose levels [P1].
